comments.author: @billeed4732
comments.text:
What many travelers may not know is that my beautiful country is also deeply affected by corruption. It's one of the main reasons why so many people, not just young people leave, whether to work abroad temporarily or to build a life elsewhere.

For example, instead of spending enormous amounts on statues in Skopje (which many tourists end up making fun of), the government could have invested more in developing tourism through our historical and natural heritage. Beyond places like Stobi, Heraclea, and Kokino, North Macedonia has thousands of archaeological sites and ruins, many of which remain unexplored, neglected, or inaccessible to visitors. Sadly, there have also been cases of archaeological artifacts ending up on the black market and leaving the country.

replies.author: @billeed4732
replies.text:
I also forgot to mention another part of our heritage that deserves far more attention: North Macedonia is home to hundreds of historic Orthodox churches and monasteries, many of them dating back centuries. Some estimates place the number of churches and monasteries (above 1,000 across the country).  Beyond the famous Ohrid—often called the "Jerusalem of the Balkans" because of the legend that it once had 365 churches, one for every day of the year—there are countless remarkable religious sites scattered throughout the country.
For example, the cave monastery church of St. Archangel Michael in Radožda, perched high above the shores of Lake Ohrid, dates back to the 13th century and contains medieval frescoes that are several centuries old. Beyond its historical significance, it offers one of the most breathtaking views of the lake and the surrounding mountains.
It's places like these that make me feel North Macedonia's tourism potential is still far from fully realized.
